name: Delmore Effect
description: A claimed tendency to formulate clearer, more articulate goals for narrow or lower-priority areas than for broader, higher-stakes ambitions. The label's exact meaning varies across internet bias lists.
design_relevance_note: At most a loose productivity/prioritization metaphor for strategy or roadmap conversations. I found no established peer-reviewed design or psychology literature behind the label itself.
myth_risk_note: Search returned zero on-topic candidates for either backing or dispute -- every candidate was an unrelated homonym or topical-drift result (hepatitis C virology, moral-contagion social psychology, pharmacogenetics replication, software-engineering methodology). Combined with the existing corpus's no_rigorous_backing_found status and the thin overall candidate count (7, versus the usual 16), this is strong, consistent evidence the named effect lacks any identifiable peer-reviewed empirical origin.
prevalence_note: I found it only on recent internet bias-list pages and design-pop-psych sites, not as a mainstream term in UX canon or peer-reviewed psychology.
